Messages.Author: Huruem
Messages.Body:
Blooded Sand a écrit :

> On Nov 26, 5:09 am, "Miriadel" <miria...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >-snip- is from the Swiss Academy, -snip-
> What is the Swiss academy?

It's a kind of joke that was developped in the french forums to
describe how Amiel developped his playgroup, trying to make the better
decks ever, and to train them to win tourneys.

Amiel is a former Magic the gathering player who was one of the first
French/swiss player to play in a pro tour and so on... So he actually
reproduced what he has done with magic in V:TES.

What characterises this "Academy" is the deckbuilding. Lots of very
straightforward decks, between 60 and 70 cards, never bigger (the only
exception is a Schambling horde/liquidation deck) to focus on a good
cardflow and to have the good cards soon. The second rule is, get rid
of the defense if it's not really useful all the time, especially for
combat defense. And the most important rule is, never play a deck which
hasn't won several tourneys. The only one who allows himself not to
respect that rule is Amiel, but he is a fucking good deckbuilder.

The other thing is that they talk a LOT, to try to get some help when
they're stuck by a prey or a predator. Not trying to find help in the
cards, but in the other players. The result is that they're dealing a
lot of VPs very often, which is something that European people tend to
like I think, Especially in big tourneys like that.

But this academy is just a joke in the sens that lots of people are
playing this way in Strasbourg, and that this way of deckbuilding comes
from Julien Moisi, another Strasbourg guy, who actually became a friend
of Amiel and corresponded together about deckbuilding a lot. I did with
them too.

So lots of people began joking about this academy saying that these
guys were just nice, but were playing really badly (which was the case
at the beginning) and won just because their decks were really good,
but still were so straightforward that each time they had an intercept
or a rush deck as a prey or predator, they just couldn't win. And lots
of good players from Sabbat in France did, I actually come from this
"academy" lol.

I think that's all, cheers !

Arthur,
missing the time when he was killing his Swiss predator...

Messages.Author: ben...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:


Presumably in non-tournament play they build their own decks and
experiment. For tournament play, I can totally understand this
method
helping them, particularly if they're a younger playgroup. I always
advise
newer players to try out the tried-and-true decks first before trying
to
experiment, because it's far easier to build esoteric decks (and
counter-
strategies to the tried-and-true) once you've gotten a handle on
what's
known to be effective.

Also, from a tournament perspective, there's certainly something to
be
said for making sure you're always playing a top-tier deck. You'll
generally have a better chance of winning if you bring a top-tier
deck than
if you bring something non-standard and less tested.

Whether or not this is _fun_ is entirely subjective. I can certainly
understand someone enjoying the challenge of trying to win
tournaments
and trying to be the best player out there. I can also appreciate
wanting
to try other ideas and other cards, be it for maximizing the
utilzation of
your collection, exploring the possibilities of the game, or just for
fun's
sake.

- Ben Peal

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman
Messages.Body:
XZealot wrote:



Yeah. I can understand it, for some people winning is the only important
thing. Winning with a "pre-constructed" deck not of your own making would
seem like a cheap victory to me. Matter of taste -- and of course, no deck
plays itself, the player skill is a big factor.

In any case, the above way of playing it pretty much anathema to the way I
play it. I'd rather lose with an interesting deck than win with cheese.
Especially if it's someone else's cheese. Again, of course, purely a matter
of taste.

Of course, that does result in me losing most of the time. :)

EC was an interesting experience. I now understand why the other Finnish
players have been saying that French players can be a problem, and
that "you can't play the game if more than one French guy is at the table,
they will play in collusion no matter what the game situation is".
Apologies to the French players who don't do that, but I have yet to meet
them, sadly enough. They're fine if there's only one at the table. Two or
more, and it's a done deal that they'll team up. It's just the way the game
is apparently played with them, but sadly it steps over the line into
illegal collusion way too often. Proving collusion is always a bitch, of
course, even when it's blatant. I guess it's the reason some of those guys
get away with it. That, and the fact that the worst offenders are the "well
known" players, so the judges apparently tend to look the other way a lot.
Oh well. Sucks, but what can you do.

For example, one French player (playing a Shambling Horde deck) actively
gave his prey (another French player) an Assault Rifle. What's the worst
enemy of a SH deck? That's right, an Assault Rifle. This in addition to
doing *nothing* offensive towards his prey, until a judge was called in..
after which he started doing token "bleed for 1s" until the judge left,
then the circus started again. Disclaimer: this is an account from players
at that game who I trust (who were totally pissed off, once again), didn't
see it personally. Saw a lot of stuff like that myself, elsewhere.

As a second disclaimer: the French players weren't the only ones that were
guilty of this. They were just the most consistent at it (and apparently
have been on previous years, too). Collusion with someone just because they
are your friend, or have the same nationality as you, seriously sucks. I
wish there was a way to get warnings and game bans for the worst offenders,
but that would require lots of judges who are on the ball -- and this
tournament didn't have those.

If the above offends someone, then it does. I'm just calling things the way
I see them. *As people* almost everyone at the EC was nice. What I have
issue with it the playing style of some of them, nothing more nothing less.

That said, most of the games were fun, some were *very* fun. Maybe too many
VP deals for my liking, ones made ridiculously early in the game ("let's
split the table 3-2" on round 4, give me a break...). I'll have to make a
t-shirt that says "shut the fuck up and play the game", if I attend EC
again :}. On the other hand, some of the dealmaking was fun and most of the
players were very cool and (mostly) friendly. The pressure got to some, I
guess, and some tried to vent their frustrations on the other players. Most
didn't.

Met a lot of cool people I had previously only met online (the Tatus, Paolo,
etc etc). Good times. Got lots of ideas, deck tips, and strategy tips. My
Laibon Harbringer/!Salubri deck didn't really work on the last chance
qualifier game (I was already qualified and was playing more a "fun" deck),
but the anarch Daughters of Cacophony deck I was playing on EC first day
did ok for such a "low-power" deck (2 VPs). Still needs tuning, but I like
the thing; when it worked it generated Echo votes like crazy. When it
didn't work was when I was sandwiched between a total of 12 static votes on
(I think) round 3. Yikes. Should have made a deal with my prey, but the
table situation kept shifting. :). On day 3 I played an Ahrimanes rush deck
which in the end only got 0.5 VPs from a stalled game, but was *really*
close to a lot more on the 2 other rounds (one was a matter of one missing
press, the other a matter of a cross-table rescue of Nergal who
turbo-chewed through the table after that). One of the guys on the stalled
game gave me some attitude about playing too slowly, which was imho
*mostly* unjustified -- yes, I was seriously sleep-lagged and probably
played a bit slower than usual, but otoh I was still playing a lot faster
than the guys who were interrupting each action with a table VP deal
proposition. Oh well, I guess he was just frustrated about the game
stalling, turns out all his 3 games had timed out. None of my other games
had, so I'd personally also lay blame on his deck; he was playing a Gangrel
intercept/earth meld deck, with very little forward pressure. Nice deck,
but decks like that tend to result in longer games. His bitching left a
slightly bad taste in my mouth, but he seemed like a nice guy otherwise.

So... yeah, was worth the trip. I'm not wild about the style of playing that
seems to be dominant in central Europe, but most of the time it doesn't
bother the game too much and you can just (try to) tell the worst
motormouths to shut up and play the game. I'm not sure what the tournament
play style is like in the U.S., but by playing with Eric, David Tatu and
other U.S. guys I got the feeling it would be more to my liking. Those
games felt a lot more relaxed and pleasant to me, even though everyone
*was* playing to win. It's a difference in player attitudes, I guess.

Oh, and we made the plane back home with only minutes to spare. But that's
another story. :)

//Petri

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman
Messages.Body:
Johannes Walch wrote:

> That´s really unecessary dicky to accuse the judges of "looking the
> other way". Unless you can prove it rather keep it to yourself. The
> people at the EC did not put hundreds of hours in the organization only
> to be seriously offended in a public forum afterwards. If you want to
> continue enjoying ECs, you should be more encouraging to the organizers.

True. That came out too strong, and I apologize. I do think there was some
small room for improvement on the judge area in that they could have been
stricter towards collusion (issued official warnings), and in that the
rules knowledge was a bit spotty at times. However, having personally run
lots and lots of big tournaments over the years, I know full well how
hectic things can get, and it's all to easy to get confused about the
various rulings in the heat of things. The "I know this, but there's a hole
in my head right now" effect. :) That, and with N players and just a few
judges there is no way they can keep an eye on everything.

Overall, the organizing was ok. There was some confusion and hassle that
could have been avoided (the debacle with the Silence of Death death lists,
etc etc), but hassle always happens. I have no real complaints on that
score.

And again, I've run and organized a *lot* of tournaments, some very big; I
know what the realities of that are. Overall, the EC organizers did a good
job, and I apologize for partially blaming them for something that's a
player problem. I'm just a bit frustrated, is all.

>> For example, one French player (playing a Shambling Horde deck) actively
>> gave his prey (another French player) an Assault Rifle. What's the worst
>> enemy of a SH deck? That's right, an Assault Rifle. This in addition to
>> doing *nothing* offensive towards his prey, until a judge was called in..
>> after which he started doing token "bleed for 1s" until the judge left,
>> then the circus started again. Disclaimer: this is an account from
>> players at that game who I trust (who were totally pissed off, once
>> again), didn't see it personally. Saw a lot of stuff like that myself,
>> elsewhere.
>
> How did the guy with the Shambling Hordes give his prey an Assault
> Rifle? I am sure he has none in the deck and then it escapes me how you
> can *give* somebody an Assault Rifle. And even more interesting I think
> I know both guys and saw the game and in that game the guy with the
> Assault Rifles was the predator of the guys with the Shamblings.
>
> Nothing is better than second hand experiences spread in public forums :)

True, that. I'll ask one of the players who was there to comment on the
details, if he wants to. I think the Swedish girl (damn, don't remember
name) was in that game too. I got the impression that he could have blocked
with no danger to himself, but didn't, but could be wrong. Remember, this
was on top of the predator doing pretty much nothing against his prey
during the game.

Of course, you could just claim it's some fiendishly clever tactic. That's
the problem with game collusion, it's a bitch to actually prove. As a
player you know it for what it is when you see it, but *prove* it beyond a
shadow of doubt? Hard. When I'm judge I tend to be very hardline about this
kind of thing (if the player cannot justify his actions he gets a warning),
but that's up to the event judges in every case.

>> As a second disclaimer: the French players weren't the only ones that
>> were guilty of this. They were just the most consistent at it (and
>> apparently have been on previous years, too). Collusion with someone just
>> because they are your friend, or have the same nationality as you,
>> seriously sucks. I wish there was a way to get warnings and game bans for
>> the worst offenders, but that would require lots of judges who are on the
>> ball -- and this tournament didn't have those.
>>
>> If the above offends someone, then it does. I'm just calling things the
>> way I see them. *As people* almost everyone at the EC was nice. What I
>> have issue with it the playing style of some of them, nothing more
>> nothing less.
>
> Do you have any solution for the problem (assuming the fact that the
> problem is indeed existing as you describe it, which some people might
> argue)? Or are you just ranting?

Well, a general solution is difficult, and to a small extent I am ranting
about what I think is an unhealthy direction for the game to go in.

But I think the removal or modification of the withdraw rule in VEKN
tournaments that LSJ is proposing in another thread is one solution. It's a
lot harder to do effective collusion and table VP deals if you can't get VP
by withdrawing (or by having it give only 0.5 VP). Lessent the incentive,
at least.

As for it being a problem... well, dunno. I personally don't like it when
people start dividing the table based on real-life friendships and other
things instead on in-game stuff, but of course it always happens to some
extent. That "some extent" is the thing, here... normally it stays in
control, but the EC was the first tournament where I've seen VP dealing and
collusion get (in my opinion) a bit out of hand.

Basically, it circumvents the designed "predator-prey" mechanic of the game
and turns it into "play for a few rounds and then start making deals on how
we divide the VPs here". That in itself is just annoying, but when those
deals start being made based on real-life friendships it becomes a problem.

I'm not the only one who complained about this at the EC, in fact I was
*far* from the only one, and I've heard similiar complaints from previous
years. Based on the fact that LSJ is proposing rule changes that would
hinder VP deals, I gather he finds it a problem too (at least in some
cases). I gather there were some related problems at this year's NAC, too.

> To my understanding it´s only natural that you ally with the guys you
> know on a given table, because normally you HAVE to ally with somebody
> and the people you can judge best (because you played them before and
> probably know that they usually keep their end of the agreement) are the
> first choice. Probably it seems worse with the French because they are a
> really big group so it is more likely to encounter more than one of them
> at a single table and they have some kind of language barrier. But I am
> very sure that it isnt worse than with any other country.

That could be. I do think there is a playing culture in France that
encourages this type of thing (or maybe some of the better-know players
encourage it, because they like to play that way).

It's funny, when Finns (or Danes, or...) play with others on the table, if
anything they are *more* brutal towards each other than they are
to "strangers". With the French it's the opposite. :)

But you're right, for players who play mainly by making VP deals, they
obviously will prefer friends and people they know, because deals with them
feel more trustworthy. It's a thin line between that and illegal collusion,
and even if it's crossed I'm not sure the players themselves always realize
it. It's not black/white.

> > I'm not sure what the tournament
> > play style is like in the U.S., but by playing with Eric, David Tatu
> > and
> > other U.S. guys I got the feeling it would be more to my liking. Those
> > games felt a lot more relaxed and pleasant to me, even though everyone
> > *was* playing to win. It's a difference in player attitudes, I guess.
>
> Those were the "Pack Alphas". I had bad experiences in the US just as in
> every other place I played.

I have no doubt of that. And I'd like to emphasise that most of my play
experiences at the EC were very pleasant. Maybe that's why the ones that
were not stand out so much. :/

//Petri

"Petri Wessman" <nos...@orava.org> wrote in message

>> Victory through Net-Decking is the parable of wisdom as I understood

>>

>
> Yeah. I can understand it, for some people winning is the only important
> thing. Winning with a "pre-constructed" deck not of your own making would
> seem like a cheap victory to me.

I don't know that winning or losing is the point where net-decking is
concerned. If you can win through net-decking (or even, as in my case,
just do better than you would otherwise) then it certainly behooves you to
consider it - at least to the degree that your deck choice reflects your
desire to win. A CCG being what it is, everybody has their idea of how
much emphasis to put on winning vs. how much to put on their desire to
play the type of deck they like. But there has to be some emphasis on
winning or there's no point to playing.

One thing I particularly like about net-decking: it gives me the opportunity
to learn how to play styles I wouldn't normally gravitate torwards in my
deck-building. Especially when my skill at building decks torwards those
styles are currently lacking. (In my case, read combat-oriented decks.
YMMV.) Using a deck built by someone who has considerable skill in those
styles is very helpful, both torwards learning to play and build those sorts
of deck and learning what their weakness are so that when I go back to my
own preferences, I know better how to deal with them.

As for whether such a victory is 'cheap' or otherwise, the distinction you
make is entirely meaningless to me. As far as I even understand it. It
seems like incredibly misplaced pride to worry about who created the deck
with which you won.

Fred

Part of learning a language is accepting that idioms exist and it's
probably a good idea to learn the more popular ones. (Like I'm a great
authority on learning languages. Much as I would love to, it's another
one my great non-skills...) "Your mileage may vary" refers to the fact
that each person has a different, very personal experience of certain
aspects of life. In my post, it referred to the fact that different
people are good or bad at different aspects of V:tES, thus which style
of deck it would be beneficial for them to consider net.decking will
likewise vary.

The term, "Your mileage may vary", has its genesis in a legal
requirement for automobile manufacturers to place the estimated urban
and freeway gas mileage estimates of each new car on its legally required
MSRP sticker which must by law be placed in each new automobile sold in
America. Included in that estimate is an inevitable clause which refers
to the point that real gas mileage observed is very dependent on the
person's driving habits and other factors. In short, even though the
MSRP sticker promises that a new car will get 'X' miles per gallon,
that person's observed experience may turn out to be different. His
mileage will vary. That ubiquitous clause on MSRP stickers has now become
an American language idiom.

Fred

Large, high profile tournaments have been won by combat decks. Heck,
the NERQ was won two years in a row by combat decks.

People don't play them a lot in large, high profile tournaments as they
are not as easy to win with as, say, S+B decks or whatever. And as a
result of not as many people playing them, they are less likely to win
across the field. But that doesn't mean that they can't win. And the
ability to make table split deals or not is mostly irrelevant to this.
